accuracy.evidence: Matches the English national curriculum Year 4 Electricity statements (name cells, wires, bulbs, switches and buzzers; a switch opens and closes a circuit; a bulb lights only in a complete loop) and the Year 6 brightness idea. Physics checked: two identical bulbs in series each get half the voltage so both are dimmer, parallel branches each get the full cell voltage, and a battery is two or more cells.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the one-wire 'source-sink' model (step 1 prediction and challenge item 7), 'an open switch lets electricity out', 'battery and cell are the same thing', 'the second bulb in series is just as bright' and 'unscrewing one parallel bulb puts the others out'. The adult notes name each slip and add the hidden cost that a parallel circuit drains the cell faster.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagseries is a circuit board you build up: a six-tile component finder, two tappable gaps to close, a switch, then an add-a-bulb slot that goes in series on the bottom wire or on a parallel branch, with unscrewable bulbs and animated current dashes. It passes the 30% shingle gate against flagcirc (ammeter and voltmeter readings) and flagcond (testing materials).

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step changes one thing in the same circuit: naming parts, then the complete loop, then the switch gap, then a second bulb in series (both dim to the same level and both go out when one is unscrewed), then the same bulb on a branch (full brightness, and the other stays lit). The live caption under the board states the rule each time the learner acts.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions are locked in before the evidence: battery versus cell, whether one wire is enough, what the open switch does, how bright two series bulbs are and how bright a parallel bulb is. Each wrong option is a known misconception, and the step reveal line quotes the learner's guess and says why it is right or wrong.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions map every wrong option to a targeted why() reply, for example 'That is parallel. In series there is only one path', 'One is a cell. A battery is two or more cells joined together', 'Open makes a gap, like a broken bridge' and 'Current must go out of one end and back into the other. One wire is not a loop'.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences built round the key words (component, cell, battery, current, voltage, conductor, insulator, series, parallel) and pass the learner kid FK gate. Adult paragraphs quote the curriculum, list the terms and name the common mistakes in short sentences that pass the learner adult gate.

no_filler.evidence: No stock phrases: every sentence either defines a term, states a rule about loops, gaps, series or parallel, or names a mistake. The family tip points at fairy lights, a torch and a remote, real things at home where the learner can spot switches, cells and series or parallel wiring.

mobile.evidence: Walked through on iPhone 13 in dark and light themes: the six component tiles sit in a two-column grid with big tap targets, the circuit board fits the width with labels clear of the glowing bulbs, and the add, unscrew and switch buttons wrap onto full-width rows under the board.

accessibility.evidence: axe reports no violations in light and dark themes. The canvas has an aria-label, every gap, switch and bulb action has a matching button, the live caption describes which bulbs are lit in words (not only by glow), and the challenge feedback sits in a polite live region.
